prompt: You know an image contains a library at a version with a published advisory, and the scan of the image reports nothing for it. Which explanation fits how an image scanner works?

choices.text: The layer holding it was cached, so the scanner skipped it
choices.why: A scanner reads every layer of the image it is given; the build cache plays no part in a scan.

choices.text: It was copied in with no package record beside it
choices.why: Right. A scanner reads the lists package managers leave; a file no list mentions is invisible to it.

choices.text: Its files are compressed, and the scanner cannot open them
choices.why: The scanner does not open the library's files at all. It reads records such as the dpkg database and METADATA files.

choices.text: The advisory was published after the image was built
choices.why: The database is what has to know the advisory, not the image. An advisory newer than the image is found by any scan after it reaches the database.

prompt: How did Trivy learn that the pip inside `python:3.13` carries urllib3 2.7.0?

choices.text: From the Debian package database in `/var/lib/dpkg`
choices.why: pip in that image was not installed by dpkg; the Debian database does not list it or what it contains.

choices.text: By comparing the files of urllib3 with known releases
choices.why: Trivy does not recognise code by its bytes, which is why the copy with no list was invisible.

choices.text: From pip's `METADATA`, which lists its requirements
choices.why: pip declares no requirements: it ships its libraries inside itself instead of depending on them.

choices.text: From `bom.cdx.json`, the SBOM pip ships in `pip/_vendor`
choices.why: Right. 18 of the image's packages were found by reading that list.

prompt: You scan an image by its digest, the same digest a colleague scanned a week ago, and you get more findings than they did. What changed?

choices.text: The image: a digest can point at new layers after a push
choices.why: A digest is the hash of the content; the same digest is the same bytes, today and in a year.

choices.text: The database
choices.why: Right. Advisories were published during the week, and your scan read a database that knows them.

choices.text: The severity threshold Trivy applies on each machine
choices.why: Severity comes from the advisory's data, and no threshold was given; both scans counted everything.

choices.text: Trivy samples files, so two scans read different ones
choices.why: Trivy reads the package records completely, every time; there is no sampling.

prompt: Which of these would an image scanner such as Trivy fail to see? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a tool downloaded with `curl` in a `RUN` line
choices.why: Right: no package manager installed it, so no record names it.

choices.text: a Debian package installed with `apt-get`
choices.why: dpkg records it in its database, which is the first list a scanner reads.

choices.text: a library copied into the repository without its metadata
choices.why: Right: vendored code with no record is what `blind:code` showed.

choices.text: a C program compiled in the build stage and copied across
choices.why: Right: a C binary records nothing about what it was built from.

choices.text: a Go program compiled in the build stage and copied across
choices.why: Go records its module dependencies inside the binary, and Trivy reads that record.

prompt: How many Debian findings did the scan report for `python:3.13`?
Going from `python:3.13-slim` to the distroless image moved the Debian count only from 164 to 162. What did the move change that the count does not show?

choices.text: It removed glibc and OpenSSL, which carry most findings
choices.why: Both are still there: distroless keeps the core libraries, which is why the count hardly moved.

choices.text: Nothing; the two images are equivalent for security
choices.why: The shell, apt and pip are gone, and with pip went the six findings that had a fix.

choices.text: No shell, apt or pip left, nor pip's fixable findings
choices.why: Right. The difference is in what code running in the container reaches, and in the column "with a fix".

choices.text: It fixed two Debian vulnerabilities that slim still had
choices.why: Two packages are absent, not fixed; nothing was patched.

prompt: With `--severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1`, `python:3.13-slim` exits 1. What decided it?

choices.text: Its 44 high Debian findings
choices.why: None of them has a fix, and `--ignore-unfixed` leaves every one of them out of the verdict.

choices.text: Four fixable highs inside pip
choices.why: Right: msgpack, setuptools and urllib3 inside pip, all with fixed versions.

choices.text: The image's size, above what the gate accepts
choices.why: The gate has no size rule; it judges findings.

choices.text: A rule that fails the image on any finding at all
choices.why: Then the distroless image, with 162 findings, would have failed too, and it exited 0.

prompt: A team keeps `python:3.13-slim` as the run base and adds `RUN pip install --upgrade pip` to get the gate green. Reasoning from the lesson, what is likely to happen over the following months?

choices.text: Green from now on, since pip is current
choices.why: pip is current today. Its vendored libraries will get new advisories, and the image will carry them until the next upgrade.

choices.text: Red within weeks, for the Debian findings of slim
choices.why: The Debian findings have no fix and the gate ignores those; they cannot turn it red.

choices.text: Green, then red at pip's next vendored advisory
choices.why: Right, and each time for a program linkbox never runs after the build. Removing pip from the image ends that.

choices.text: Green, because the gate does not scan pip once it has been upgraded
choices.why: The gate scans whatever the image holds, upgraded or not.

prompt: Match each status Trivy reports with what the distribution has said.

pairs.right: a newer version of the package carries the fix
vulnerable, and no fix is published for this release yet
a fix is planned and postponed
it will not be fixed in this release

right_distractors: the image was scanned before the advisory existed

prompt: The distroless image's 162 findings are how many distinct CVEs?
CVE-2024-26458 appears on four lines of the distroless report. Why four?

choices.text: The image has four layers, and each layer reports it
choices.why: A finding is reported per package, not per layer; the four packages happen to share one source.

choices.text: Four binary packages are built from one source, krb5
choices.why: Right. One upload of krb5 fixes all four, or none.

choices.text: Four vendors each scored it, and each score is a row
choices.why: Scores from several vendors are fields of one finding, not separate rows.

choices.text: Four versions of Kerberos are installed side by side
choices.why: All four packages are the same version, 1.21.3-5+deb13u1.

prompt: A weekly report counts rows of the image scan. Last week 162, this week 158, and no other row changed. What is the most that can safely be said?

choices.text: Four vulnerabilities were fixed this week
choices.why: Four rows went, which may be a single CVE in a source package that builds four binaries.

choices.text: The team fixed 2.5% of the image's risk
choices.why: Rows are not risk, and the team did not necessarily fix anything; a new base image may have.

choices.text: Something changed, perhaps a single CVE
choices.why: Right. Count distinct CVEs per source package to know more.

choices.text: Nothing changed in the image; the database dropped rows
choices.why: The database could have changed, but so could the image; the count alone cannot tell which.

prompt: Which of these turns one of the counted, no-fix findings into work for this week?

choices.text: The finding has been open for thirty days
choices.why: Age alone changes nothing a rebuild can do; the status still says no fix exists.

choices.text: It is rated MEDIUM rather than LOW
choices.why: Severity was already known when the gate decided to count it; it is not news.

choices.text: It lands in CISA KEV, on a library linkbox loads
choices.why: Right. Known exploitation of something reachable is a reason to patch or change base, whatever the gate says.

choices.text: The total rose from 162 to 163
choices.why: A new no-fix finding is still no-fix; the count moving is worth reading, not an emergency.

prompt: What does `pip install --target /packages` achieve in the build stage?

choices.text: It installs the packages for user 65532 instead of root
choices.why: Ownership is not what `--target` changes; it changes where the packages go.

choices.text: It puts the packages, and only them, in a directory of their own
choices.why: Right: that directory crosses to the run stage while pip stays behind.

choices.text: It skips the packages' compiled parts
choices.why: Compiled parts are installed as usual; that is why both stages use Python 3.13.

choices.text: It checks each package against the hashes in requirements.txt
choices.why: That is `--require-hashes`, which lesson 15 adds; `--target` is about where.

prompt: Why does the Dockerfile start the service with `python3 -m gunicorn` rather than `gunicorn`?

choices.text: Distroless images refuse to run scripts
choices.why: They run any executable; this script fails for a different reason, the interpreter its first line names.

choices.text: `-m` makes gunicorn run as a user that is not root
choices.why: The user comes from the image's `USER`, 65532 here, whatever the command is.

choices.text: Its script names a Python this image lacks
choices.why: Right. The first line of `/packages/bin/gunicorn` points at the slim image's interpreter; `python3 -m` uses the one that exists.

choices.text: gunicorn has no script in `/packages/bin`
choices.why: pip writes the script there; the problem is the interpreter it names, not its absence.

prompt: The final image has no shell. According to the lesson, what does that protect against?

choices.text: Code execution inside the container becomes impossible
choices.why: Python is still there, and it is a complete programming language.

choices.text: The easy path, and the findings of what is gone
choices.why: Right. The one-line commands most intrusions start with need a shell, and absent programs bring no findings.

choices.text: It stops anybody from running `docker exec` on it
choices.why: `docker exec` works; it just has no `sh` to start, and `python3` still runs.

choices.text: It hides the image's packages from scanners
choices.why: The scanner read all 38 Debian packages and every `METADATA` in `/packages`.

prompt: In the run stage, the line that brings the installed packages across from the first stage is: `COPY --from=___ /packages /packages`
Why does `push` come after `image` in `ci/stages`?

choices.text: So nothing reaches the registry that the scan refused
choices.why: Right: the run stops at the first stage that fails, and push never runs.

choices.text: Because Trivy can scan only images that are not in a registry yet
choices.why: Trivy scans images in a registry just as well; the order is about what may be published.

choices.text: So the registry can tag the image with the scan's result
choices.why: The registry stores what it is given; it knows nothing about scans.

choices.text: Because pushing first would make the scan slower
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the order decides what the registry may hold.

prompt: A typo in `ci/build.sh` makes it tag the image `linkbox:dev` while `ci/image.sh` scans `linkbox:<commit>`, which does not exist. What does the image stage do?

choices.text: It passes, because there is no image and so no finding
choices.why: That is the failure lesson 7 named: a scanner that did not run reporting a pass.

choices.text: It breaks the build, as a scan that did not run
choices.why: Right. Trivy exits 1 when it cannot run, `|| exit 1` stops there, and the capture with `CI_COMMIT=0000000` shows it.

choices.text: It scans `linkbox:dev` instead, the nearest match
choices.why: Trivy looks for the name it is given and nothing else.

choices.text: It warns, because a missing image is not a vulnerability
choices.why: Exit status 3 is the warning; this stage turns any trouble with the scan into a break.

prompt: Google republished the distroless image yesterday with a fixed glibc. Tonight `ci/nightly` runs its `docker build --no-cache`. Does linkbox's image get the fix?

choices.text: Yes: with no cache, every layer is rebuilt, the base included
choices.why: Every layer of the Dockerfile is rebuilt; the base image is reused from the machine, as it was.

choices.text: Yes, because the gate fails until the base is updated
choices.why: The gate scans what was built; it does not fetch a newer base.

choices.text: Not unless the build asks the registry again, with `--pull`
choices.why: Right. `--no-cache` reuses the local base; `--pull` fetches the tag's current image. Lesson 15 makes the base a digest instead.

choices.text: No: distroless images are never updated under the same tag
choices.why: They are; `:nonroot` is a tag that moves when Google rebuilds it.

prompt: The option of `docker build` that asks the registry for the current image behind each `FROM` tag, instead of reusing the copy on the machine, is `docker build ___`
Put what happens to an image in one passing run of the pipeline in order, from first to last.
items: built and tagged with the commit
scanned for fixable high and critical findings
every finding counted into the log

prompt: Which statements about the image this lesson ships are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: it runs as user 65532
choices.why: Right: the distroless `nonroot` variant sets it.

choices.text: it has pip, for installing a hotfix in place
choices.why: pip stayed in the build stage, on purpose.

choices.text: its scan still counts 162 Debian findings
choices.why: Right: the floor of the distroless base, counted in every run's log.

choices.text: the application can rewrite its own `app.py`
choices.why: The code is owned by root and the process is 65532; only `/data` is its own.

choices.text: it carries no high finding that has a fixed version
choices.why: Right, which is what the image stage checks on every push.
